`docs/pages/concepts/batching-and-flushing.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Batching and flushing"
description: "When reliable traffic actually leaves, how big batches are split, and how to take control of the timing."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Batching and flushing

## Reliable traffic is batched

A reliable `Fire` does not call the remote. It appends a frame to an outgoing buffer for that peer: one buffer per player on the server, one on the client. Once per frame, the **replication step** sends each non-empty buffer as a single remote call. Twenty events to one player in one frame cost one remote call, and every reliable event to a peer arrives in the order it was fired.

Broadcasts (`FireAll`, `FireList`, `FireExcept`, `FireGroup`) encode the data once and copy the bytes into each recipient's buffer.

## The replication step

By default the step runs on `RunService.Heartbeat`. On each run it:

1. expires [invokes](/concepts/functions-and-invokes) that passed their timeout;
2. on the server, issues [integrity challenges](/security/client-integrity) and samples [characters](/security/character-integrity);
3. on the server, flushes pending [channel](/concepts/state-channels) state into the buffers;
4. sends each peer's buffer, if the flush rule allows.

The flush rule sends a peer's buffer when any of these holds:

- at least 1/60 of a second has passed since that peer's last flush;
- the buffer has reached [`MaxBurstBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxburstbytes);
- the peer's tracked queue is at least half of [`MaxQueuedBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxqueuedbytes).

At the usual 60 Hz heartbeat, that means every frame.

## Taking control

With [`ManualReplication`](/reference/options/runtime#manualreplication) the step is not connected, and you call [`StepReplication`](/reference/api/module#stepreplication) yourself. Use it to flush after your simulation step, or at a lower rate for a game that does not need per-frame traffic.

```lua copy
RunService.PostSimulation:Connect(function()
    Simulation.Step()
    Network.StepReplication()
end)
```

<Callout type="warning">
Timeouts, integrity challenges, character checks and channel flushes all run inside the step. If you stop calling it, they stop too.
</Callout>

## Unreliable traffic is not batched

Each unreliable `Fire` is sent immediately as its own `UnreliableRemoteEvent` call, capped by [`MaxUnreliablePacketBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxunreliablepacketbytes). This keeps unreliable data as fresh as possible, but it means a hundred unreliable events cost a hundred remote calls. If you send many small unreliable updates, combine them into one event carrying an array.

## Fragmentation

Roblox limits how much one remote call can carry. When a reliable batch is larger than [`ReliableFragmentBytes`](/reference/options/limits#reliablefragmentbytes) (48 KB by default), it is split into fragments sent as separate calls and reassembled on arrival. Reliable delivery keeps them in order.

A batch larger than [`MaxReliablePacketBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxreliablepacketbytes) is not fragmented; it is dropped whole on the sender with `MaxPacketBytes`. Keep individual events well below that cap, and use a [channel](/concepts/state-channels) or several events for large state.

```

`docs/pages/concepts/functions-and-invokes.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Functions and invokes"
description: "How request and reply work, and how to keep invokes from hanging."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Functions and invokes

A [`function`](/reference/declarations/function) is a request a client makes and the server answers. The server never invokes clients, so a client can never hang a server thread.

## The round trip

1. The client calls `Invoke`. The request is written into the client's reliable batch with a one-byte invocation id, and the calling thread yields (or a Future or Promise is returned).
2. At the next replication step the batch is sent.
3. The server receives the request, runs it through the [receive pipeline](/concepts/receive-pipeline), and calls the function's `On` handler in a new thread.
4. The handler's return values are written into that player's batch and sent at the server's next step. If the handler errors, or its return value cannot be encoded, a failure reply is sent instead.
5. The client matches the reply to the invocation id and resumes the caller.

A round trip therefore takes at least one frame on each side plus the network latency.

## Failures

Every request gets an answer: a reply, a failure reply with a reason, or a timeout.

| What happened | `Invoke` raises |
| --- | --- |
| The server dropped the request before the handler ran (policy, auth, constraint, cooldown, rate limit, kill switch, replay, malformed payload, queue full) | `[Cheeto]: The server rejected "Name": <reason>`, with the drop reason, or the reason your policy returned |
| The handler errored, or returned something that does not fit the `Return` type | `[Cheeto]: The server rejected "Name": HandlerError` |
| The client dropped the reply, for example because it exceeds the [decode budgets](/reference/options/limits#decode-budgets) | `[Cheeto]: The reply to "Name" was dropped: <reason>`, straight away |
| No reply within the timeout | `[Cheeto]: Invoke timed out after N seconds.` |
| Too many invokes pending | Immediately, before anything is sent |
| The request could not be encoded (a value out of range, a wrong enum) | Immediately, with the encoding error |
| [`CancelInvocations`](/reference/api/module#cancelinvocations) was called | The reason you passed |

The one exception is [`Honeypot`](/reference/fields#honeypot) functions: nothing legitimate calls them, so the server stays silent and the caller times out.

The timeout is the function's [`InvokeTimeoutSeconds`](/reference/fields#invoketimeoutseconds) field if it has one, otherwise the runtime's [`InvokeTimeoutSeconds`](/reference/options/limits#invoketimeoutseconds): 10 seconds under `Production`, 5 under `Competitive`, none under `Development`, or what `Configure` last set.

```cheeto copy
option SecurityProfile = Production

function GetShopStock {
    Yield: Coroutine,
    Policy: "shop",
    CooldownSeconds: 1,
    Return: u16[..64]
}
```

```lua copy
local ok, result = pcall(Network.GetShopStock.Invoke)
if not ok then
    warn("Shop unavailable:", result)
end
```

## Choosing a yield style

| `Yield` | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| `Coroutine` | You call from a thread that may yield, and want the value directly |
| `Future` | You use red-blox's Future library |
| `Promise` | You use evaera's Promise library and want chaining and cancellation |

## Limits

- At most [`MaxPendingInvokes`](/reference/fields#maxpendinginvokes) outstanding per function and per module.
- At most 256 outstanding per module, because invocation ids are one byte.
- Replies are discarded if the player leaves before the handler returns.

```

`docs/pages/concepts/how-it-works.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "How Cheeto works"
description: "From schema to generated modules to remote calls, and what each piece is responsible for."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# How Cheeto works

## The compiler

The `cheeto` compiler reads a schema, checks it, and writes:

| Output | Option | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server module | [`ServerOutput`](/reference/options/output#serveroutput) | Senders for server-origin endpoints, listeners for client-origin ones, channel writers, and the server runtime |
| Client module | [`ClientOutput`](/reference/options/output#clientoutput) | The mirror image, plus the client runtime |
| Types module | [`TypesOutput`](/reference/options/output#typesoutput) | Shared Luau types, optional |
| `.d.ts` files | [`Typescript`](/reference/options/output#typescript) | roblox-ts declarations, optional |
| Shared runtime | [`RuntimeOutput`](/reference/options/output#runtimeoutput) | The runtime as its own module, optional |

The modules are ordinary ModuleScripts with no dependencies other than the Future or Promise library if you use them. Commit the schema and regenerate the modules; do not edit generated code.

## Two remotes

When the server module is first required, it creates two instances in ReplicatedStorage: a `RemoteEvent` for reliable traffic and an `UnreliableRemoteEvent` for unreliable traffic. Every endpoint in the schema shares them. Each message carries a one-byte endpoint number so the receiver knows which endpoint it belongs to. Endpoint names never go over the wire.

The client module waits for those two remotes and connects to them. With [remote name rotation](/security/remote-hardening) on, they live in a folder and get random names.

## Sending

When you call `Fire`:

1. The endpoint's [`BeforeSend`](/reference/api/hooks#beforesend) hooks and [kill switch](/reference/api/security#kill) are checked.
2. The data is written into a buffer as a **frame**: a small header followed by the payload, packed according to the schema.
3. **Reliable** frames are appended to that peer's outgoing batch. Once per frame (on `Heartbeat`), the runtime sends each peer's batch as one remote call, splitting it into fragments if it is very large. See [Batching and flushing](/concepts/batching-and-flushing).
4. **Unreliable** frames are sent immediately, one remote call each.

Instances cannot be written into a buffer, so they travel as a list in the remote call's second argument.

## Receiving

When a remote call arrives, the runtime checks the whole packet (size, rate, type of arguments), then reads it frame by frame. Each frame passes a sequence of checks (rate limits, auth, policy, decoding, validation) before its listener runs. A frame that fails any check is dropped and reported, and the runtime moves to the next frame. Nothing throws into your code. See [The receive pipeline](/concepts/receive-pipeline).

## What runs where

The runtime inside each module holds all the state: outgoing batches, listener tables, rate-limit buckets, capture buffers, security scores. Two modules never share state, even with a shared runtime module. Configure and register rules on the module that does the receiving: policies on the server module, samplers on the client module.

<Callout type="info">
Each side's module must be compiled from the same schema. There is no negotiation between different schemas; see [Schema versioning](/concepts/schema-versioning).
</Callout>

```

`docs/pages/concepts/interest-and-routing.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Audiences and routing"
description: "Groups, zones, distance, parties, matches and other ways to choose who receives data."
---

# Audiences and routing

Sending everything to everyone wastes bandwidth and can leak information. Cheeto keeps several kinds of membership you can target sends at.

## Groups

Named sets of players, used by [`FireGroup`](/reference/api/event#firegroup) and channel `SetGroup`, `PatchGroup` and `FlushGroup`.

```lua copy
Network.SetGroup("RedTeam", redPlayers)
Network.AddToGroup("Spectators", player)
Network.TeamChat.FireGroup("RedTeam", sender.Name, text)
```

See [`SetGroup`](/reference/api/module#setgroup) and related functions.

## Zones and distance, per channel

Channels can target players by zone or by distance. You tell the runtime where players are; it does not track characters itself.

```lua copy
-- Zones: set when a player enters or leaves an area
Network.AreaWeather.SetInterestZone(player, "Desert")
Network.AreaWeather.SetZone("Desert", { Kind = "Sandstorm", Intensity = 3 })

-- Distance: update positions, then send around a point
Network.Explosions.SetInterestPosition(player, root.Position)
Network.Explosions.SetDistance(origin, { Position = origin, Radius = 20 }, 300)
```

Setting [`Interest: Zone`](/reference/fields#interest) or `Interest: Distance` on the channel makes the shorthand `Set` and `Patch` use these variants.

## Parties, matches, teams, cells and owners

[`Network.Replication`](/reference/api/replication) keeps further memberships, read with `GetInterestPlayers`:

```lua copy
Network.Replication.SetParty(partyId, player)
Network.Replication.SetMatch(matchId, player)
Network.Replication.SetTeam("Red", player)
Network.Replication.SetStreamedCell("cell_4_7", player)
Network.Replication.SetObjectOwner(vehicle, player)

for _, member in Network.Replication.GetInterestPlayers("Party", partyId) do
    Network.PartyInvite.Fire(member, inviter)
end
```

`Team` also includes every player whose Roblox `Team` has that name, so `SetTeam` is only needed for teams that are not Roblox teams.

Events have no dedicated fire method for these; pass the list to `FireList`. Channels do: a channel with [`Interest`](/reference/fields#interest) or [`Scope`](/reference/fields#scope) set to `Party`, `Match`, `Team`, `Cell` or `Owner` maps its `Set`, `Patch` and `Flush` to that membership, and every channel has `SetScope`, `PatchScope` and `FlushScope` for any kind:

```cheeto copy
struct SquadData {
    Objective: string,
    Score: u16
}

channel SquadState {
    Interest: Party,
    Data: SquadData
}
```

```lua copy
Network.SquadState.Set(partyId, { Objective = "Hold B", Score = 12 })
Network.SquadState.SetScope("Match", matchId, { Objective = "Final round", Score = 0 })
```

## Routing graphs

A [`Graph`](/reference/api/replication#graph) lets one system keep its own observer lists that override the shared memberships, for example spectators who watch a match they are not in.

## Cleanup

Every membership is removed automatically when a player leaves. Memberships that change during play, such as a player leaving a party or a zone, are yours to update.

## Across servers

[`Replication.MessagingService`](/reference/api/replication#messagingservice) and [`Replication.MemoryStore`](/reference/api/replication#memorystore) wrap Roblox's cross-server services with the same group, zone and match naming, and tag every message with the schema version.

```

`docs/pages/concepts/prediction.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Prediction"
description: "Act immediately on the client, then confirm or undo when the server answers."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Prediction

Prediction lets a client show the result of an action before the server confirms it, and undo it if the server refuses. Cheeto tracks the pending predictions and tells you when each is confirmed or rolled back.

## The flow

1. The client calls the event's [`Predict`](/reference/api/event#predict) instead of `Fire`. It sends the event with a prediction id and returns the id.
2. The client applies the action locally, remembering the id.
3. The server receives the event. If it decodes successfully, the server automatically sends back an acknowledgement; if decoding fails, it sends a rejection with the reason.
4. On the client, an acknowledgement calls [`Prediction.Ack`](/reference/api/prediction#ack) and a rejection calls [`Prediction.Rollback`](/reference/api/prediction#rollback), which run the [`Ack`](/reference/api/hooks#ack) and [`Rollback`](/reference/api/hooks#rollback) hooks.

```lua copy filename="Client.client.luau"
local placed = {}

Network.Use("Ack", function(context)
    placed[context.Id] = nil
end)

Network.Use("Rollback", function(context)
    local block = placed[context.Id]
    if block then
        block:Destroy()
        placed[context.Id] = nil
    end
end)

local function place(position)
    local id = Network.PlaceBlock.Predict(position)
    placed[id] = Blocks.CreateGhost(position)
end
```

## What the acknowledgement means

The acknowledgement is sent when the event **decodes**, before your server listener runs. It confirms that the server accepted the data, not that your game logic succeeded. If your listener can still refuse the action, send your own result event and roll back from it.

<Callout type="warning">
A predicted event the server drops, by a policy, auth rule, constraint, cooldown, rate limit, kill switch or replay check, is answered with the reason, and the prediction rolls back with it. A [`Latest`](/reference/fields#reliabilitymode) prediction replaced before it was sent rolls back with `Superseded`. Only a lost connection leaves a prediction pending; [`Prediction.Pending`](/reference/api/prediction#pending) lists them.
</Callout>

## Sequence numbers

The prediction id doubles as a sequence number, which is what enables [replay protection](/security/replay-and-idempotency) and [`Idempotency`](/reference/fields#idempotency) for that event. Events sent with `Fire` have no sequence number and get neither.

## Turning it off

With [`EnablePrediction`](/reference/options/runtime#enableprediction) set to `false`, `Predict` is not generated, unless an event sets `Predict: true`, and the prediction helpers error at runtime.

```

`docs/pages/concepts/receive-pipeline.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "The receive pipeline"
description: "Every check a received packet and event go through, in order, and what each drop means."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# The receive pipeline

This is the exact order in which a received remote call is checked. Knowing it tells you what can see what: a policy runs before decoding, so it cannot read the payload; a `Validate` hook runs after, so it can.

## 1. The packet

For each remote call:

| Step | Check | On failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The first argument is a buffer | `InvalidBuffer` |
| 1b | The sender's handshake did not name another schema | `IncompatibleProtocol` |
| 2 | Its size is within [`MaxReliablePacketBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxreliablepacketbytes) or [`MaxUnreliablePacketBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxunreliablepacketbytes) | `MaxPacketBytes` |
| 3 | The sender is within the per-call [`RateLimitPerSecond`](/reference/options/limits#ratelimitpersecond) for this remote | `RateLimit` |
| 4 | The second argument, if any, is a table of instances | `InvalidInstances` |
| 5 | Packet-level [`BeforeReceive`](/reference/api/hooks#beforereceive) hooks allow it | `MiddlewareRejected` |
| 6 | Reliable only: if it is a fragment, it is stored and processing stops until the last fragment arrives | `FragmentOverflow`, `FragmentTimeout`, `MalformedPacket` |

Any failure here discards the whole call.

## 2. Each frame

The packet is then read one frame at a time. Control frames (handshake, prediction acknowledgements, fragments, shield and integrity messages) are handled internally. For every endpoint frame:

| Step | Check | On failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The frame header can be read; for a function, the invocation id too | `MalformedPacket` |
| 2 | The frame is within the endpoint's own [`MaxPacketBytes`](/reference/fields#maxpacketbytes), if set | `MaxPacketBytes` |
| 3 | The endpoint is not a [honeypot](/security/honeypots) | `Honeypot` |
| 4 | The sender is within the endpoint's [`RateLimitPerSecond`](/reference/fields#ratelimitpersecond), if set | `RateLimit` |
| 5 | Per-event [`BeforeReceive`](/reference/api/hooks#beforereceive) hooks allow it | `MiddlewareRejected` |
| 6 | The [`Auth`](/reference/fields#auth) rule returns `true`, if set | `AuthRejected` |
| 7 | The endpoint and its policy group are not [killed](/security/kill-switches) | `KillSwitch` |
| 8 | The sender's [`CooldownSeconds`](/reference/fields#cooldownseconds) has elapsed | `Cooldown` |
| 9 | Predicted events only: the prediction id is new and recent | `ReplayDuplicate`, `ReplayStale` |
| 10 | Predicted events with [`Idempotency`](/reference/fields#idempotency): the prediction id was not used in the last 120 s | `ReplayDuplicate` |
| 11 | The sender [constraints](/security/constraints) hold: team, zone, match, character state | `ConstraintRejected` |
| 12 | The [`Policy`](/reference/fields#policy) allows the sender, or with [`RequirePolicies`](/reference/options/security#requirepolicies) the endpoint has a policy, group or auth rule | `PolicyRejected` or the policy's reason |
| 13 | Every policy in the [`PolicyGroup`](/reference/fields#policygroup) allows the sender | `PolicyRejected` or the policy's reason |
| 14 | The payload **decodes**: types, ranges and instance classes all match | `MalformedPacket` |
| 15 | [`Sequenced`](/reference/fields#reliabilitymode) and [`Idempotency`](/reference/fields#idempotency) endpoints: the sequence number is newer than the last accepted | `OutOfOrder` |
| 16 | The decoded payload passes the [payload checks](/security/payload-validation) | `Canonicalization`, `DecodeBudget` |
| 17 | The payload [constraints](/security/constraints) hold: distance, ownership, handles, known ids, inventory | `ConstraintRejected` |
| 18 | [`Validate`](/reference/api/hooks#validate) hooks allow it, if the endpoint declares a payload constraint | `ConstraintRejected` |
| 19 | [`AfterReceive`](/reference/api/hooks#afterreceive) hooks run; predicted events are acknowledged | |
| 20 | The listener runs, or the event is queued if no listener is connected yet | `QueueFull` when the queue is full |

When the server drops a function call or a predicted event at any of these steps (except a honeypot), it answers with the reason: `Invoke` raises it and the prediction rolls back with it.

A failed frame is skipped using its length prefix, and the next frame is processed normally.

## What this means for your code

- **Policies and auth rules cannot see the payload.** Steps 6 to 13 run before step 14. Check "who" in a policy and "what" in a `Validate` hook or in the listener.
- **Honeypots report even rate-limited senders.** Step 3 comes before the rate limit, so a flood of honeypot traffic is fully reported.
- **Cooldowns cost almost nothing.** A request inside its cooldown is rejected before any decoding work.
- **Your listener only sees valid data.** By step 20, the payload matches the schema's types and ranges and passed your rules.

<Callout type="info">
The frame steps run on whichever side receives the endpoint. That is why `Auth`, `Policy`, cooldowns, idempotency and constraints are compile errors on server-sent events and channels: the client has none of the server's rules.
</Callout>

```

`docs/pages/concepts/reliability-and-priority.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Reliability and delivery"
description: "Reliable and unreliable events, the Sequenced and Latest delivery modes, batching, and what Priority does."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Reliability and delivery

## Reliable or unreliable

| | `Type: Reliable` | `Type: Unreliable` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arrives | Always, unless dropped by a check | Usually; can be lost |
| Order | In order with every other reliable event to that peer | Any order, unless `Sequenced` |
| Sent | Batched, once per replication step | Batched per recipient once per step ([`BatchUnreliable`](/reference/options/runtime#batchunreliable)), or immediately with it off |
| Size | Up to `MaxReliablePacketBytes`, fragmented above 48 KB | Up to `MaxUnreliablePacketBytes` (about 1 KB) per batch |
| Queued before a listener connects | Yes | No, discarded |

Use **reliable** for anything whose loss would be a bug: purchases, damage, state changes, chat. Use **unreliable** for data that is replaced by the next update anyway: positions, aim, cosmetic effects. Losing one is harmless, and waiting for a retransmission would only deliver stale data.

Functions are always reliable. [Channels](/concepts/state-channels) are reliable unless you set `Type: Unreliable`.

## Delivery modes

[`ReliabilityMode`](/reference/fields#reliabilitymode) refines how an event is delivered:

| Mode | Behaviour | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(none)* | Every send is delivered (reliable) or may be (unreliable) | Most events |
| `Sequenced` | Each send carries a sequence number; anything not newer than the last accepted is dropped with `OutOfOrder` | Unreliable positions, where an old value arriving late is worse than none |
| `Latest` | Only the last send per recipient in each replication step leaves; the rest are discarded before they cost bandwidth | Aim direction, health bars, anything that is overwritten several times a frame |

[`CoalesceKey`](/reference/fields#coalescekey) is `Latest` with a slot shared by every event that names the same key, for state described by several endpoints.

```cheeto copy
event AimDirection {
    From: Client,
    Type: Unreliable,
    Call: ManyAsync,
    ReliabilityMode: Latest,
    Data: vector
}

event Position {
    From: Server,
    Type: Unreliable,
    Call: ManyAsync,
    ReliabilityMode: Sequenced,
    Data: vector<i16>
}
```

## Batching

Reliable events queue in each recipient's batch and leave together at the replication step, which runs on `Heartbeat` unless you use [`ManualReplication`](/reference/options/runtime#manualreplication). Unreliable events do the same by default, one remote call per recipient per step, split so no call exceeds `MaxUnreliablePacketBytes`. Fewer, larger calls cost less and keep high-frequency traffic under the receiver's per-call [rate limit](/reference/options/limits#ratelimitpersecond). The cost is up to one frame of delay.

## Priority

[`Priority`](/reference/fields#priority) has four levels: `Critical`, `Gameplay` (the default), `Cosmetic` and `Background`.

Priority decides one thing: which events may be **shed** when a peer is backed up. Each peer's queued bytes are counted as events are copied into its batch and reset when the batch is sent. When they exceed [`MaxQueuedBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxqueuedbytes) and [`LowPriorityShedding`](/reference/options/limits#lowpriorityshedding) is on, new `Cosmetic` and `Background` events to that peer are dropped with `Backpressure`. `Critical` and `Gameplay` events are never shed.

Priority does not reorder events within a batch or send them sooner.

```cheeto copy
event HitSpark {
    From: Server,
    Type: Unreliable,
    Call: ManyAsync,
    Priority: Cosmetic,
    Data: vector<f16>
}
```

<Callout type="info">
Broadcasts are counted per recipient, when they are copied into each player's batch. A player who is falling behind sheds low-priority broadcasts; the others are unaffected.
</Callout>

```

`docs/pages/concepts/schema-versioning.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Schema versioning"
description: "Changing a schema safely while servers and clients are live."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Schema versioning

The server and its clients must run modules compiled from the same schema. Normally they do: when you publish, new servers start with the new modules, and clients joining them download the new client module. Problems start when that assumption breaks, for example with long-lived servers during a rollout, or with data you stored using an old layout.

## What changes the wire

Anything that changes the bytes of a message:

- changing an endpoint's id: removing or reordering endpoints without a lockfile, or editing a [`WireId`](/reference/fields#wireid);
- changing a field's type, order, range or optionality, or an endpoint's channel or delivery mode;
- changing [encoding options](/reference/options/encoding).

Changes that do not affect the wire: whitespace, comments, renaming a type alias, reordering endpoints while `cheeto.lock` is present, and options that only affect limits or security.

## The fingerprint and the handshake

Every build carries a [fingerprint](/reference/options/versioning#the-schema-fingerprint) of its wire layout. With the [handshake](/reference/options/versioning#enableprotocolhandshake) on, both sides exchange it, and the server stops decoding a player whose fingerprint differs from its own, because those packets would be read against the wrong layout. Set [`IncompatiblePeerAction = Kick`](/reference/options/versioning#incompatiblepeeraction) to kick them with a message asking them to rejoin.

```cheeto copy
option IncompatiblePeerAction = Kick
```

`Protocol.Info(player).Peer` shows what a player reported, for logging:

```lua copy
local peer = Network.Protocol.Info(player).Peer
if peer and not peer.Compatible then
    warn(player.Name, "runs schema", peer.SchemaHash, "; the server runs", Network.Schema.Hash)
end
```

## Version numbers

[`Version`](/reference/options/versioning#version) is a number you choose, sent in the handshake and stamped on captures and saved state. You do not need to raise it for the handshake to notice a wire change, but it gives you a readable number in logs and lets [`MinimumSchemaVersion`](/reference/options/versioning#minimumschemaversion) turn away old builds explicitly.

```cheeto copy
option Version = 7
option MinimumSchemaVersion = 7
```

## Keeping ids stable

Commit [`cheeto.lock`](/reference/lockfile). The compiler reads it and gives every endpoint the id it had before, so reordering endpoints or removing one does not renumber the rest; a removed endpoint stays in the lock as retired and its id is never reused. For ids that must never move, pin them with [`WireId`](/reference/fields#wireid).

To rename or renumber an endpoint without breaking builds that still use the old id, give it a [`DeprecatedId`](/reference/fields#deprecatedid): the endpoint is sent under its new id but still accepted on the old one.

```cheeto copy
event Purchase {
    From: Client,
    Type: Reliable,
    Call: SingleAsync,
    WireId: 12,
    DeprecatedId: 4,
    Data: u32
}
```

## Reviewing changes

Run `cheeto --check-lock` in CI. It fails, listing the lines that changed, whenever an endpoint is added, removed or renumbered, or a payload type changes shape, until someone regenerates the lockfile with `--write-lock`. That puts every wire change in front of a reviewer.

## Stored data

Data you saved with an [exported type](/reference/api/exports) keeps its old layout forever. Store the version next to it, and upgrade on load with [`Schema.Migrate`](/reference/api/schema#migrate):

```lua copy
Network.Schema.RegisterMigration(6, function(save)
    save.Coins = save.Gold
    save.Gold = nil
    return save
end)

local save, version = Network.Schema.Migrate(loaded.Data, loaded.Version)
```

```

`docs/pages/concepts/state-channels.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "State channels"
description: "Replicate server-owned state as snapshots and deltas instead of events."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# State channels

Many things clients need are **state**, not events: a player's health, a match's scoreboard, a door's open or closed flag. Sending an event for every change works, but a client that joins late, or misses an update, never catches up. A [`channel`](/reference/declarations/channel) solves this: the server holds the value, sends it to clients in full when needed and as small deltas otherwise, and clients can always read the latest value.

## Snapshots and deltas

```cheeto copy
channel Scoreboard {
    Scope: Global,
    TickRate: 10,
    Data: struct {
        Red: u16,
        Blue: u16,
        TimeLeft: u16
    }
}
```

```lua copy filename="Server.server.luau"
Network.Scoreboard.Set({ Red = 0, Blue = 0, TimeLeft = 600 })  -- full snapshot to everyone

Network.Scoreboard.Patch({ Red = 1 })       -- only Red is sent
Network.Scoreboard.Patch({ TimeLeft = 599 }) -- merged with the pending patch
```

- `Set` stores the whole value and schedules a **full snapshot**.
- `Patch` merges fields into the stored value and marks only those fields dirty. The next flush sends a **delta**: a bitmask saying which fields changed, then just those fields.
- Several patches before a flush are merged, so only the latest value of each field is sent.

Flushing happens automatically in the replication step, at most [`TickRate`](/reference/fields#tickrate) times per second. [`KeyframeRate`](/reference/fields#keyframerate) forces periodic full snapshots. `Flush*` sends immediately.

Deltas need a struct `Data`. For any other type, every flush sends the full value.

## Per-player state

With `Scope: Player` (the default), the server stores a separate value per player, and `Set`/`Patch` take the player first:

```lua copy
Network.PlayerState.Set(player, { Health = 100, Stamina = 100 })
Network.PlayerState.Patch(player, { Stamina = 80 })
```

The targeted variants (`SetAll`, `SetList`, `SetGroup`, `SetZone`, `SetDistance` and their `Patch` and `Flush` versions) work for every channel regardless of `Scope`. See [Channel endpoint](/reference/api/channel).

## Reading on the client

```lua copy filename="Client.client.luau"
local function render(board)
    Ui.Score.Text = `{board.Red} - {board.Blue}`
end

local current = Network.Scoreboard.Get()
if current then
    render(current)
end
Network.Scoreboard.On(render)
```

`On` fires after every snapshot or delta, with the full current value, a version counter, and the patch for deltas.

<Callout type="info">
`On` does not replay the value that arrived before you connected. Read `Get()` first, as above, or use [`Connection:OnState`](/reference/api/connection#onstate) with `fireImmediately`.
</Callout>

## When to use an event instead

Use events for things that happen (a hit, a message, a purchase) and channels for things that are (health, score, settings). A channel only ever delivers the latest value, so intermediate values between two flushes are never seen.

```

`docs/pages/concepts/wire-protocol.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Wire protocol"
description: "The byte layout of Cheeto packets and frames."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Wire protocol

Cheeto has one wire format. There is nothing to negotiate and nothing to configure; what the two sides do compare is the [schema fingerprint](/reference/options/versioning#the-schema-fingerprint), which changes whenever an endpoint's id, channel or payload does.

You do not need this page to use Cheeto. It is here for debugging captures and for contributors.

## Packets

A **packet** is one remote call. Its first argument is a buffer; its second is either `nil` or an array of instances.

The buffer is a sequence of **frames**, one per event, function call, reply or control message, back to back.

## Frames

| Field | Size | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Index | 1 byte | Which endpoint this frame belongs to (0 to 251), or a control frame (252 to 255) |
| Flags | 1 byte | Bit 0: a prediction id follows |
| Payload length | varint | Bytes of payload after the header |
| Instance count | varint | How many entries of the instance array belong to this frame |
| Prediction id | varint | Only when flag bit 0 is set |
| Payload | *length* bytes | The values, encoded per the schema |

Reliable and unreliable endpoints are numbered separately. An endpoint keeps the index pinned by [`WireId`](/reference/fields#wireid) or recorded in [`cheeto.lock`](/reference/lockfile); new endpoints take the lowest free index in declaration order. Because every frame states its length, a receiver can skip a frame it rejects and continue with the next, which is how one bad event never affects the others in its packet.

## Example

`DealDamage.Fire({ Target = target, Damage = 25 })`, for an event whose data is `{ Target: Instance(Player), Damage: u16(0..500) }`:

| Bytes | Field |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Index of `DealDamage` |
| `00` | Flags: no prediction id |
| `01` | Payload length: 1 byte |
| `01` | Instance count: 1 (`Target`) |
| `19` | `Damage = 25` as a varint |

Five bytes in the buffer, plus `target` in the instance array.

## Payload encoding

Values are written in schema order with no field names or type tags:

- `u8`/`i8` as one byte; 16 and 32-bit integers as LEB128 varints (zig-zag for signed) when [`UseVarints`](/reference/options/encoding#usevarints) is on, otherwise little-endian fixed width.
- `f16`, `f32`, `f64` as IEEE floats, little-endian.
- Booleans and optional presence flags as bits, eight per byte, when [`UseBitPacking`](/reference/options/encoding#usebitpacking) is on.
- Strings and buffers as a length then the bytes; exact-length types have no length. With [`UseStringDictionaries`](/reference/options/encoding#usestringdictionaries), each string starts with a varint marker: `0` for a literal, `1` for a literal the receiver remembers for the rest of the packet, `n ≥ 2` for the (n−1)th remembered string.
- Arrays and maps as a count then the elements; a ranged map's count uses only the bytes its maximum needs.
- `Sequenced` and `Idempotency` endpoints start their payload with a 16-bit sequence number (after the invocation id, for a function call).
- Unit enums as a one-byte index; tagged enums as the index then the variant's fields.
- Instances and `unknown` values in the instance array, not the buffer.

See [Types](/reference/types/numbers) for each type's layout.

## Function calls

A call frame uses the function's index. Its payload is the invocation id (`u8`), then the sequence number if the function has `Idempotency`, then the arguments.

## Function replies

A reply frame uses the function's index. Its payload is the invocation id (`u8`), then a success byte: `1` followed by the return values, or `0` followed by the reason (a string with a one-byte length). The reason is the drop reason when the call never reached the handler, or `HandlerError`.

## Control frames

| Index | Purpose | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 255 | Prediction reply | Prediction id (varint), accepted (bit), reason (string) |
| 254 | Capability handshake | Format marker (`u8`), format (`u8`), schema version (`u16`), minimum version (`u16`), fingerprint length (`u8`), fingerprint |
| 253 | Fragment | Fragment id, index, count and original size (varints), then a slice of the original packet |
| 252 | Shield and integrity | A kind byte (0 shield report, 1 challenge, 2 receipt) and its fields |

## Fragmentation

A reliable batch larger than [`ReliableFragmentBytes`](/reference/options/limits#reliablefragmentbytes) is cut into slices, each wrapped in a fragment frame and sent as its own remote call. The receiver collects slices by fragment id and processes the reassembled packet once every slice has arrived. Reassembly is bounded by [`MaxInFlightFragments`](/reference/options/limits#maxinflightfragments) and [`FragmentTimeoutSeconds`](/reference/options/limits#fragmenttimeoutseconds).

<Callout type="info">
The byte layout depends on the [encoding options](/reference/options/encoding). Both sides read them from their own configuration, so they must agree.
</Callout>

# Installation

Cheeto ships as a single self-contained binary for Windows, macOS and Linux, as a [pesde](https://pesde.dev) package, and as a Roblox Studio plugin. Pick whichever fits your workflow; every option compiles the same language.

## Command-line compiler

<Tabs items={['Rokit', 'pesde', 'Manual']}>
<Tabs.Tab>

```sh copy
rokit update pealz1/cheeto

pesde runs the compiler through Lune, so you do not need a separate binary.

</Tabs.Tab>
<Tabs.Tab>

</Tabs>

```

`docs/pages/getting-started/introduction.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Introduction"
description: "What Cheeto is, how it works, and where to find everything."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Introduction

Cheeto is a networking compiler for Roblox. You describe your game's network traffic once, in a small schema language, and Cheeto generates two Luau modules: one for the server and one for the client. They contain typed functions for every message, the code that packs those messages into buffers, and the checks that reject bad data before your code sees it.

```cheeto copy filename="network.cheeto"
option ClientOutput = "Network/Client.luau"
option ServerOutput = "Network/Server.luau"

event DealDamage {
    From: Client,
    Type: Reliable,
    Call: SingleAsync,
    Policy: "combat",
    CooldownSeconds: 0.25,
    Data: struct {
        Target: Instance(Player),
        Damage: u16(0..500)
    }
}
```

```lua copy filename="Server.server.luau"
local Network = require(ReplicatedStorage.Network.Server)

Network.Security.RegisterPolicy("combat", function(context)
    return context.Source.Character ~= nil
end)

Network.DealDamage.On(function(player, hit)
    Combat.Apply(player, hit.Target, hit.Damage)
end)
```

```lua copy filename="Client.client.luau"
local Network = require(ReplicatedStorage.Network.Client)

Network.DealDamage.Fire({ Target = target, Damage = 25 })
```

## Why use it

- **Smaller packets.** Every message is written into a buffer at its declared width, integers as variable-length numbers and booleans as bits. Reliable messages to a player are batched into one remote call per frame.
- **Types on both sides.** The generated functions are fully typed, so a wrong argument is an autocomplete error, not a runtime surprise. TypeScript definitions are available for roblox-ts.
- **Data is checked before it reaches you.** Ranges, instance classes, sizes, rate limits and your own policies are enforced as each message is received. Invalid messages are dropped and reported; they never throw into your handlers.
- **One place for the contract.** The schema is the single definition of what can be sent, by whom, and how often. Reviewing a network change means reading one diff.

## How it works

1. You write a `.cheeto` schema with [options](/reference/options/overview) and [declarations](/reference/declarations/event): events, functions, channels and types.
2. The `cheeto` compiler, or the [Studio plugin](/getting-started/studio-plugin), turns it into a server module and a client module.
3. The server module creates one `RemoteEvent` and one `UnreliableRemoteEvent`. Every message in the schema travels through these two, identified by a one-byte number.
4. Your code requires the modules and calls typed functions such as `Fire` and `On`.

See [How Cheeto works](/concepts/how-it-works) for the details.

## Where to go next

| If you want to | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Install the compiler | [Installation](/getting-started/installation) |
| Build a first schema | [Quick start](/getting-started/quick-start) |
| Understand what happens to a message | [The receive pipeline](/concepts/receive-pipeline) |
| Lock down client requests | [Security model](/security/overview) |
| Look up an exact option, field or function | [Reference](/reference) |
| Know what Cheeto cannot do | [Limitations](/limitations) |

<Callout type="info">
Cheeto has one wire format, with nothing to choose or configure. What the two sides compare is a fingerprint of your schema, so a client and server built from different schemas never misread each other.
</Callout>

```

`docs/pages/getting-started/quick-start.mdx`:

```mdx
import { Callout, Steps } from 'nextra/components'

# Quick Start

This guide walks through writing, compiling and using your first network description. It uses the command-line compiler, but the language is identical in the Studio plugin.

<Steps>

### Describe your network

Create a file called `network.cheeto` and add an event:

```cheeto copy filename="network.cheeto"
-- Output paths are relative to this file. In the Studio plugin they are
-- relative to the instance you choose to generate into.
option ClientOutput = "src/shared/Network/Client.luau"
option ServerOutput = "src/shared/Network/Server.luau"

event Announce {
    From: Server,
    Type: Reliable,
    Call: SingleSync,
    Data: string
}
```

Every event declares who sends it (`From`), how it travels (`Type`), how listeners are called (`Call`) and what it carries (`Data`). The [event](/reference/declarations/event) reference covers every field.

### Compile it

From the directory that contains the file, run:

```sh copy
cheeto network
```

Cheeto finds `network.cheeto`, validates it and writes two modules: `Client.luau` and `Server.luau`. Add `--watch` to recompile automatically whenever the file or any of its imports change.

### Use the generated modules

Each module returns a frozen table containing your events and functions, fully typed.

```lua copy filename="Server.server.luau" {3}
local Network = require(ReplicatedStorage.Network.Server)

Network.Announce.FireAll("Hello from the server!")
```

```lua copy filename="Client.client.luau" {3-5}
local Network = require(ReplicatedStorage.Network.Client)

Network.Announce.On(function(message)
    print(message)
end)
```

</Steps>

<Callout type="info">
  Generated files are build output. Commit the `.cheeto` source and regenerate instead of editing the modules by hand.
</Callout>

## Where to go next

- See every option, field and type in the [Reference](/reference).
- Protect what clients send with the [Security model](/security/overview).
- Get a schema ready to ship with the [Production checklist](/operations/production-checklist).

```

`docs/pages/guides/comparison.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Comparison"
description: "How Cheeto compares with Zap, the closest schema-compiled networking library."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Comparison with Zap

[Zap](https://zap.redblox.dev) is the library closest to Cheeto: both compile a schema into typed Luau modules that pack data into buffers. If you know Zap, most of Cheeto's language will look familiar.

<Callout type="info">
This page compares documented features, as of this release. Where Zap's documentation does not cover something, the table says so instead of guessing.
</Callout>

## Shared ground

Both libraries have:

- a schema language with events (`from`, `type`, `call`, `data`) and functions;
- reliable and unreliable events, with the same five call styles (`SingleSync`, `SingleAsync`, `ManySync`, `ManyAsync`, `Polling`);
- buffer serialization, batching of reliable events per frame, and a manual replication mode;
- Luau types, TypeScript definitions, output casing options, remote scoping and microprofiler labels;
- write-side type checks as an option;
- Future and Promise support for functions.

## Where they differ

| | Zap | Cheeto |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Option style | `snake_case` in the schema | `PascalCase` |
| Function yield style | One global `yield_type` | Per function, with `Yield` |
| Rate limits and cooldowns | Not documented | Per remote call and per endpoint |
| Auth rules and policies before decoding | Not documented | Yes |
| Middleware hooks | Not documented | 13 hooks, including post-decode `Validate` |
| Honeypot endpoints | Not documented | Yes |
| Kill switches | Not documented | Per endpoint and per policy group |
| Payload budgets (depth, keys, string length, NaN) | Not documented | Yes |
| Server-side movement checks, client tripwires, liveness challenges | Not documented | Optional |
| State channels with delta patches | Not documented | Yes |
| Client prediction with server acknowledgement | Not documented | Yes |
| Reliable fragmentation of large batches | Not documented | Yes |
| Version handshake and lockfile | Not documented | Yes: a schema fingerprint the server enforces, and a lockfile that keeps ids stable |
| Packet capture and replay | Tooling integration for external inspectors | Built-in capture, replay and inspector |
| Metrics | Not documented | Built-in counters |
| Option to remove `FireAll` | `disable_fire_all` | No |
| Configurable remote folder | `remote_folder` | Rotation folder only |
| Studio plugin | Not documented | Yes |

## Choosing

Zap is smaller and does one thing: fast, typed serialization. If you already validate and rate-limit in your own code and want the leanest output, it is a good choice.

Cheeto generates more code (each module includes a runtime of about 135 KB) in exchange for the protections and tooling above. It suits games where clients are actively attacked and you want those defences declared in the schema rather than rebuilt per endpoint.

## Moving from Zap

- Rename options to PascalCase: `server_output` becomes `ServerOutput`, `casing` becomes `Casing`.
- `funct` blocks become `function` blocks, with a `Yield` field instead of the global `yield_type`.
- Field names can stay lowercase: Cheeto accepts `from`, `type`, `call` and `data` as well as the capitalised forms.
- Add a `Policy` and a cooldown or rate limit to every client-sent endpoint. See the [Security model](/security/overview).

```

`docs/pages/guides/controller-connections.mdx`:

```mdx
# Controller connections

Cheeto can group generated endpoints and state channels into one connection object that you create during bootstrap and inject into controllers. The connection is a lifecycle and routing layer; every message still uses the generated Cheeto endpoint, so serialization, validation, security policies, and batching are unchanged.

## Define The Typed Traffic

Keep transport data in the schema. For example:

```cheeto copy
struct UIState {
    Visible: boolean,
    Title: string(0..64)
}

event UIAction {
    From: Client,
    Type: Reliable,
    Call: ManySync,
    Policy: "ui",
    Data: string(0..32)
}

event UIMessage {
    From: Server,
    Type: Reliable,
    Call: ManySync,
    Data: string(0..128)
}

channel UI {
    Scope: Player,
    TickRate: 20,
    Delta: true,
    Data: UIState
}
```

## Create And Inject A Client Connection

Bind friendly route names to generated endpoints once, then pass the connection through each controller's `Init` method.

```lua copy
local Network = require(ReplicatedStorage.Network.Client)

local connection = Network.Connection.new({
    Routes = {
        Action = Network.UIAction,
        Message = Network.UIMessage,
    },
    State = {
        UI = Network.UI,
    },
})

for _, controller in ControllerList do
    controller:Init(connection)
end
```

The controller owns only its subscriptions and behavior:

```lua copy
function UIController:Init(connection)
    self._connection = connection

    connection:On("Message", function(message)
        self:ShowMessage(message)
    end)

    connection:OnState("UI", function(state)
        self:SetVisible(state.Visible)
        self:SetTitle(state.Title)
    end, true)
end

function UIController:Dismiss()
    self._connection:Send("Action", "Dismiss")
end
```

Passing `true` to `OnState` immediately supplies the current snapshot in addition to future changes. Use `GetState` when a controller only needs a read:

```lua copy
local currentUI = connection:GetState("UI")
```

## Bind A Server Connection To A Player

Set `Target` for a player-scoped server connection. Cheeto automatically passes that player as the first argument when the connection sends or reads state.

```lua copy
local connection = Network.Connection.new({
    Target = player,
    Routes = {
        Message = Network.UIMessage,
    },
    State = {
        UI = Network.UI,
    },
})

connection:Send("Message", "Welcome")
local currentUI = connection:GetState("UI")
```

For server-side incoming events, generated listeners still receive the sending player. A target does not filter incoming listeners; keep authorization in Cheeto policies or check the player inside the handler.

## Push State Through The Connection

`SetState`, `PatchState`, `ClearState`, and `FlushState` write to a bound channel so a controller can push an update without reaching around the connection for the raw endpoint. They follow the same targeting rule as `Send`: with a `Target` the player is supplied for you.

```lua copy
connection:SetState("UI", { Visible = true, Title = "Welcome" })
connection:PatchState("UI", { Title = "Ready" })
connection:FlushState("UI")
```

Without a `Target`, pass the player yourself, exactly as you would to `Send`:

```lua copy
local connection = Network.Connection.new({ State = { UI = Network.UI } })

connection:SetState("UI", player, { Visible = true, Title = "Welcome" })
connection:FlushState("UI") -- no target, so this flushes every subscriber
```

Writes are server-only. Client channels are read-only, so `SetState` on a client connection errors rather than silently doing nothing.

## Lifecycle And Late Binding

Connections track every subscription created by `On`, `Once`, and `OnState`. Tear down the connection when its controller group is no longer needed:

```lua copy
connection:Disconnect()
-- connection:Destroy() is an alias
```

`Disconnect` is idempotent and releases all tracked subscriptions. Sends and new subscriptions fail after teardown so stale controllers cannot silently keep using the network.

Routes and channels can also be added before injection:

```lua copy
local connection = Network.Connection.new()
    :Bind("Action", Network.UIAction)
    :Bind("Message", Network.UIMessage)
    :BindState("UI", Network.UI)
```

Every method is documented in the [Connection reference](/reference/api/connection).

```

`docs/pages/guides/integration-notes.mdx`:

```mdx
# Integration notes

Hard-won notes from putting Cheeto into real places. Everything here cost a
debugging session to learn once; none of it should cost one twice.

## Keep one source of truth, and generate the rest

The failure that gets reported as "the networking just stopped working" is almost
never the transport. It is two lists that were supposed to agree and quietly
stopped agreeing.

A real integration ends up with a schema, a group/module manifest, per-event rate
limits, cooldowns and policy names. If a human maintains more than one of those,
they will drift. Write **one** spec file and generate every other artifact from
it, including any manifest your game-side proxy reads. If a comment in your repo
says a list "MUST stay in sync" with another list, that is a bug waiting to
happen, not a convention.

A small generator script is enough: a JS object of endpoints emits every
`.cheeto` schema *and* the manifest block inside the game's `Network.luau`.
Adding an endpoint is one line in one file.

## Put per-event settings on the event

Side tables keyed by event name (`RATE_OVERRIDES`, `COOLDOWNS`, `POLICIES`, ...)
read fine with six endpoints and become unreviewable at thirty: you cannot tell
what an event's actual contract is without grepping five places. Put the settings
next to the data:

```js
Jail: { c2s: null, rate: [2, 4], cooldown: 1, policy: "HasCharacter" }
```

The value of this is not typing fewer characters. It is that the whole contract
for an endpoint is visible in one line during review.

## Fail-closed things that will silently kill an endpoint

Cheeto deliberately fails closed in several places. That is the right default,
and it means a typo removes a feature with no error at the call site. The ones
to know:

| Declaration | If the rule is not registered |
|---|---|
| `Policy: "X"` | **Every packet on that event is dropped.** |
| `PolicyGroup: "X"` | Adds no checks until registered. A policy *listed in* a registered group that is itself unregistered drops every packet. |
| `Auth: "X"` | **Every packet on that event is dropped**, and one warning is logged per unknown rule name. |

Register the rule in the same change that declares it. If your endpoints are
split across several generated modules, register on **all of them** -- a policy,
auth rule or kill switch applied to one module leaves the event live in whichever
module actually carries it.

Introduce `Auth` on a live game in report-only form first: have the rule record
and return `true`, watch the logs, and only then enforce. An auth gate that
depends on a handshake winning a race against the player's first input will drop
real traffic, and it will do it silently.

## Constraint fields are inputs to a rule you write, not enforcement

`MaxDistance`, `RequireOwnership`, `RequireTeam`, `RequireZone`, `RequireMatch`,
`RequireInventoryOwnership`, `RequireCharacterState`, `RequireObjectHandle` and
`RequireServerKnownId` are parsed, validated and handed to your own code in
`Context.Constraints`. **The runtime enforces none of them by itself.** Declaring
one without a rule that reads it does nothing at all.

There is a hard limit on what a *policy* can enforce: **policies run before the
payload is deserialised.** A policy can act on constraints about the sender
(`RequireCharacterState` -- is this player's character alive?) and cannot act on
constraints about the payload (`MaxDistance` -- how far away is the target the
client named?), because the value it would measure does not exist yet.

Payload-dependent constraints go in the **`Validate`** middleware, which runs after
decoding and before your listener; returning false drops the packet as
`ConstraintRejected`:

```lua
Network.Use("Validate", function(Context)
    -- { Name, Source, Channel, Size, Constraints, Payload }
    local Max = Context.Constraints.MaxDistance
    return not (Max and Max > 0) or WithinRange(Context.Source, Context.Payload[1], Max)
end)
```

The hook is emitted only for events that declare a payload-dependent constraint,
so events that declare none keep an unchanged receive path. Register the check in
the same change that declares the field -- a declared constraint with no rule
reading it is a silent no-op, which is exactly the trap these fields used to be.

## Anti-replay and idempotency need a sequence number

`ReplayWindowSize`, `ReplayStaleSeconds` and `Idempotency: true` all key on the
packet's sequence number, and a sequence only reaches the wire when the sender
attached a prediction id. On an event with no prediction there is nothing that
identifies one logical call, so there is nothing to deduplicate, and these are
inert no matter what you set them to.

To bound a one-shot action that carries no sequence, use `CooldownSeconds`. That
one the runtime enforces by itself, and it rejects *before* deserialising -- which
is also why it is stricter than a throttle inside your handler.

Always set a cooldown looser than the client's own retry cadence, or a legitimate
retry gets eaten. If a client re-asks every 2s, a 1s cooldown is right and a 3s
cooldown silently breaks it.

## Honeypots work because names are not on the wire

Frames carry a one-byte endpoint number, never a name, so the only way to
discover an endpoint is to read the generated client module -- which is exactly
what writing an exploit involves. That makes `Honeypot: true` genuinely useful:
give it an attractive name, never call it from game code, and any inbound traffic
is proof of a fabricated packet rather than a mistake. See
[Honeypots](/security/honeypots).

## Land client-side detection in report-only first

`EnableClientShield` with `ClientShieldKick = false` reports and scores without
removing anybody. A false positive here ejects a paying player, so watch the
violation stream from a live server before enabling kicks. The same applies to
honeypots if you wire them to a kick.

## Studio's 200,000-character script limit

The runtime is the same size whether you declare one event or a hundred, so a
large surface has to be split across modules, each under the limit. Two things
follow:

- Set `RuntimeOutput`/`RuntimeRequire` so the runtime is emitted **once** as a
  shared module instead of inlined into every endpoint module.
- Check generated sizes as a build step, not at install time. A size check
  that fails the build is far cheaper than a module Studio rejects on install.

## Do not resume a thread you do not own

Two of the nastiest bugs found in this library were the same mistake in different
clothes: acting on a thread reference without proof the thread was waiting for
*you*.

- `SyncValidation` recorded the thread that processed a packet and never cleared
  it, then called `coroutine.close` on it if it was merely `suspended`. Any thread
  that had fired an event and later waited on something unrelated could be killed.
  `coroutine.close` is not an error, so `pcall` catches nothing and the thread
  simply becomes `dead` far from the cause.
- An invocation reply selects which pending call to resolve using an identifier
  read straight off the wire. If anything threw between taking an identifier and
  reaching the yield, the entry outlived its thread, and a later packet could
  resume a thread that had since parked on something else.

If you extend the runtime, hold the same line: resume or close a thread only with
positive proof it is parked where you think it is.

```

`docs/pages/guides/migrating-from-remotes.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Migrating from RemoteEvents"
description: "Moving an existing game from RemoteEvents and RemoteFunctions to Cheeto, one remote at a time."
---

import { Callout, Steps } from 'nextra/components'

# Migrating from RemoteEvents

Cheeto can run next to your existing remotes, so you can move one remote at a time.

<Steps>

### Inventory your remotes

List every `RemoteEvent` and `RemoteFunction`, who fires it, what it carries, and what the server does with it. For each, note what could go wrong if a client sent garbage or sent it 100 times a second.

### Write the schema for one remote

Take a remote like this:

```lua filename="Before"
-- Client
ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.BuyItem:FireServer(itemId)

-- Server
ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.BuyItem.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, itemId)
    if typeof(itemId) ~= "number" then return end
    Shop.Buy(player, itemId)
end)
```

and declare it, moving the manual checks into the schema:

```cheeto copy filename="network.cheeto"
option ClientOutput = "Network/Client.luau"
option ServerOutput = "Network/Server.luau"
option RequirePolicies = true

event BuyItem {
    From: Client,
    Type: Reliable,
    Call: SingleAsync,
    Policy: "shop",
    CooldownSeconds: 0.5,
    Data: u16(1..999)
}
```

### Replace the calls

```lua filename="After"
-- Client
Network.BuyItem.Fire(itemId)

-- Server
Network.Security.RegisterPolicy("shop", function(context)
    return Profiles.IsLoaded(context.Source)
end)

Network.BuyItem.On(function(player, itemId)
    Shop.Buy(player, itemId) -- itemId is guaranteed to be a whole number from 1 to 999
end)
```

The type check, the range check and the throttle are now in the schema. Delete the old remote.

### Repeat, then tighten

Move the rest of the remotes the same way. Then add the optional protections: [`SecurityProfile = Production`](/security/maximum-security), [honeypots](/security/honeypots), and [`OnViolation`](/security/violations) logging.

</Steps>

## Translation table

| Before | Cheeto |
| --- | --- |
| `RemoteEvent`, client to server | `event` with `From: Client` |
| `RemoteEvent`, server to client | `event` with `From: Server` |
| `UnreliableRemoteEvent` | `event` with `Type: Unreliable` |
| `RemoteFunction`, client invokes | `function` |
| `RemoteFunction`, server invokes client | Not supported. Use an event each way |
| `FireAllClients` | `FireAll` |
| `FireClient` | `Fire(player, ...)` |
| `OnServerEvent:Connect` | `On` |
| Replicated `ValueBase` objects or attributes for state | `channel` |
| `typeof` checks in handlers | Schema types and ranges |
| Hand-written debounce tables | `CooldownSeconds` |

<Callout type="warning">
The server never invokes clients in Cheeto, because a client that never answers would hang a server thread. Replace server-to-client `RemoteFunction` calls with an event to the client and an event back.
</Callout>

## Things that change

- **Timing.** Reliable events are sent at the end of the frame, not the moment you fire. Code that fires and immediately expects the other side to have received it was already racing; it now races predictably.
- **Instances.** Instances that have not streamed in arrive as `nil`. Mark them optional (`Instance(Model)?`) wherever that can happen.
- **Tables.** Cheeto sends only the fields the schema declares. Extra keys in a table you fire are silently left out.
- **Errors.** Bad data from clients no longer reaches your handlers at all. If you logged suspicious input in handlers before, log it from [`OnViolation`](/security/violations) instead.

```

`docs/pages/limitations.mdx`:

```mdx
---
title: "Limitations"
description: "What Cheeto does not do, where its checks stop, and the trade-offs behind its defaults."
---

import { Callout } from 'nextra/components'

# Limitations

This page lists what Cheeto does not do, and where its checks stop. Each entry says what happens and what to do about it. Everything here is a design limit or a property of Roblox, not a known defect.

## Security

### Clients can always see and send traffic

Anything the server sends to a client can be read by that client, and anything a client can send, an exploiter can send with any values. No networking library changes this. Validate every client request on the server with [policies](/security/policies), [constraints](/security/constraints) and your own checks, and never send secrets to clients.

### Client-side detection is best-effort

The [client shield](/security/client-shield) runs on the exploiter's machine, which they control: it can be removed, hooked or fed false results. [Client integrity](/security/client-integrity) receipts use a checksum anyone can compute from the client module. Treat both as evidence and tripwires, not proof. Keep authority on the server.

### Remote names are visible to clients

[Name rotation](/security/remote-hardening) renames the same RemoteEvent instances and publishes the current names as attributes, which is how the legitimate client module finds them. Decoys share the real remotes' name format and classes, so a generic "fire everything" tool cannot tell them apart. A script written against your game's client module can still find the real pair.

### Idempotency stops replays, not new requests

[`Idempotency`](/reference/fields#idempotency) stamps every client send with a sequence number, and the server drops a packet whose number is not newer than the last one it accepted. A captured packet sent again is dropped. A fabricated packet with a fresh number is an ordinary new request: bound those with [`CooldownSeconds`](/reference/fields#cooldownseconds), rate limits and server state.

### What the payload constraints examine

The built-in [payload constraints](/security/constraints) look at the arguments and at the fields of table arguments, one level deep:

| Constraint | Examines |
| --- | --- |
| `MaxDistance` | Every `Vector3`, `CFrame`, `BasePart`, `Model` and `Attachment`; a sender without a character is rejected when any is present |
| `RequireOwnership` | Every Instance |
| `RequireObjectHandle` | The first number |
| `RequireServerKnownId` | The first number or string |
| `RequireInventoryOwnership` | Whatever your [resolver](/reference/api/security#setinventoryresolver) checks |

Deeper values, and conditions these do not express, belong in a [`Validate` hook](/reference/api/hooks#validate).

### Dropped events without a prediction get no answer

A function call or a predicted event that the server drops is answered with the drop reason. A plain `Fire` is not answered, because nothing on the client is waiting for it. If the client needs to know, make it a function or send it with `Predict`.

## Transport

### Ids depend on cheeto.lock

Endpoints keep their ids across reorders and removals only while `cheeto.lock` is next to the schema and committed, and only in builds made with the command-line compiler: the Studio plugin does not read the lock. Without it, ids follow declaration order, as they do the first time a schema is compiled. Pin ids that must never move with [`WireId`](/reference/fields#wireid). See [cheeto.lock format](/reference/lockfile).

### Mixed schemas are not decoded

The handshake compares [schema fingerprints](/reference/options/versioning#the-schema-fingerprint), and the server stops decoding a player whose fingerprint differs from its own. There is no translation between two layouts: any change to an endpoint's id, channel or payload makes old and new builds incompatible. In Roblox both sides normally come from the same place version, so this only matters for modified clients and during updates.

### Batching adds up to a frame

Reliable events, and unreliable events with [`BatchUnreliable`](/reference/options/runtime#batchunreliable) (the default), leave at the next replication step, which runs on `Heartbeat`. [`Latest`](/reference/fields#reliabilitymode) events leave then too, keeping only the last value. Turn batching off for unreliable events that must leave immediately.

### Unreliable delivery is unreliable

Unreliable events can be lost or arrive out of order, and a lost batch loses every event in it. Use [`Sequenced`](/reference/fields#reliabilitymode) to drop out-of-order arrivals, and reliable events for anything that must arrive.

### Priority only affects shedding

[`Priority`](/reference/fields#priority) decides which events are dropped when a peer's queued bytes exceed [`MaxQueuedBytes`](/reference/options/limits#maxqueuedbytes): `Cosmetic` and `Background` go first, `Critical` and `Gameplay` never. It does not reorder a batch or change when it is sent.

### Payload checks apply to everything

The [decode budgets](/reference/options/limits#decode-budgets) apply to every endpoint in both directions. Strings over 8,192 bytes and tables over 2,048 keys are dropped by default, even when the schema allows them. Raise the budget options when a schema legitimately needs more.

### Endpoint and invoke counts

Endpoint ids are one byte with four values reserved for control frames, so a schema supports at most 252 reliable and 252 unreliable endpoints; the compiler rejects more. At most 256 invokes can be outstanding per module.

### Studio's script size limit

Studio rejects scripts over 200,000 characters. Each generated module contains the runtime (about 200 KB) unless you use [`RuntimeOutput`](/reference/options/output#runtimeoutput). Split large surfaces across several schemas with a shared runtime. See [Large schemas](/operations/large-schemas).

## Schema language

### Delta channels need a struct

A channel sends patches only when its data is a struct, because a patch names fields. Any other data type is always sent whole.

### Generic types cannot be exported

An `export` declaration cannot be generic. Export a concrete instantiation through an alias, for example `type Pair = Generic<u8, u8>`.

## Tooling

### Benchmarks run in Lune

[`--benchmark`](/reference/cli#--benchmark) and [`--load-sim`](/reference/cli#--load-sim) run the generated modules in Lune against stub remotes, with generated sample payloads and the schema's access rules removed. The byte counts are exact; the timings are Lune on your machine, which is close to but not the same as a Roblox server. Endpoints whose types have no sample (for example `DateTime`) are reported as skipped.

### TypeScript types for the runtime are structural

The generated `.d.ts` files describe every endpoint precisely. The runtime namespaces (`Security`, `Transport` and the rest) are typed from the reference, with `unknown` where a value depends on the schema. Roblox types such as `Instance` and `Vector3` come from `@rbxts/types`.

<Callout type="info">
Found something missing from this page? [Open an issue](https://github.com/pealz1/cheeto/issues).
</Callout>
